claims.statement: Keycloak is the MCM platform's only authority for user identities and OAuth2 token issuance: it runs as the `keycloak-service` container with a dedicated Postgres (`keycloak-store-postgres`) in the `auth` Docker Compose project, and is deployed in production as the Komodo `prod-auth` stack whose `after = []` root position makes it the first stack in the deploy order. The realm is `grumpyrobot`, the user-facing login client is `movie-collection-manager`, and the platform RBAC unit is that client's roles `mc-user` and `mc-admin` — they are CLIENT roles read from `resource_access[movie-collection-manager].roles`, so assigning the same-named realm role is a no-op that yields an authenticated user with an empty role list.

Keycloak's app port is published as host `8099` mapped to container `8080` and bound to loopback in dev/CI, while containers on the shared Docker network must reach it as `keycloak-service:8080`; feature 020 unified the Compose service key and `container_name` to `keycloak-service`, so the older bare `keycloak` name no longer resolves.

The realm exists in three committed variants that import through three separate paths into the same Postgres volume: `dev-realm.json` via the `compose.dev.yaml` overlay on `pnpm nx up-auth infrastructure-as-code`, `ci-realm.json` via the `compose.ci.yaml` overlay in app-ci's Keycloak bring-up step, and `prod-realm.json` via `compose.prod.yaml` under Komodo. Only the dev and CI overlays add `--import-realm`, leaving the shared `keycloak/compose.yaml` base and therefore the CI path unchanged. (The namespace of committed filenames is separate from the import namespace: every variant is mounted at the target path `grumpyrobot-realm.json`.)

A mounted realm file MUST land at `<realmName>-realm.json` (`grumpyrobot-realm.json` here) or Keycloak's directory import aborts with a file-name/realm-name mismatch — the committed source filenames (`dev-realm.json`, `ci-realm.json`, `prod-realm.json`) are never the import path. Relatedly, Compose resolves a RELATIVE volume source against the PROJECT directory (the directory of the first `-f`, i.e. `docker/stacks/`), not the overlay file's own directory, so the dev overlay uses `../keycloak/dev-realm.json` while CI and prod each pass an absolute path (`${CI_REALM_FILE}`, `${PROD_REALM_FILE}`); a bare `./ci-realm.json` silently made Docker create an empty DIRECTORY at that path.

Realm import is idempotent and non-destructive because Keycloak's directory import IGNORE_EXISTING semantics skip a realm that already exists: an established `keycloak-store-postgres-data` volume is untouched on every `up-auth`, and a fresh or wiped volume gets the `grumpyrobot` realm, its app clients, and `e2e-test-user` re-seeded on the next `up-auth`. The same property means an edit to a realm JSON file changes nothing for a stack that is already running until the realm is re-imported.

The three realm variants deliberately differ in `accessTokenLifespan`: `ci-realm.json` and `dev-realm.json` both carry 5400 s while `prod-realm.json` carries 300 s. CI's 90-minute value exists because Playwright reloads a frozen `storageState` snapshot in a fresh `BrowserContext` per test, so a 300 s token expires five minutes into a run and forces every later test through a refresh path measured at a 1.9 s median against the BFF's 2-per-30 s per-session limit (35 of 115 attempts rejected); 5400 s outlives the 75-minute `app-e2e` job timeout. Dev was raised to match (feature 054) after two 44-minute local runs recorded 62 `refresh_rate_limited` and collapsed into `gotoHome: home screen did not render`; the refresh path's local coverage was traded away and is now covered instead by `tests/integration/rate-limiter.integration.test.ts`. Production's 300 s is unchanged, so no security control is relaxed.

The token-exchange wiring for the agent layer lives in the realm: `standard.token.exchange.enabled` on the confidential `agent-gateway` and `agent-subject-token` clients, per-client `access.token.lifespan` ceilings (60 s for the gateway's exchanged token, 180 s for the run-scoped subject token), audience mappers making the downscope targets available, and an `agent_origin=true` hardcoded-claim mapper on both. Two Keycloak standard-exchange-v2 preconditions make the mappers load-bearing: the requester must appear within the subject token's `aud` (else `access_denied: Client is not within the token audience`), and the `audience` request parameter can only select an audience the requester can already produce (else `invalid_request: Requested audience not available`). All added mappers are additive — both the BFF and mc-service use contains/intersection audience checks, so extra `aud` entries are ignored by components that do not need them.

Realm JSON files reject unknown fields: Keycloak deserializes them into `RealmRepresentation` with unknown properties rejected, so an explanatory key such as `_comment_accessTokenLifespan` fails the import, leaves the container unhealthy, and kills every dependent job at bring-up (measured on app-ci run 1611, feature 052). JSON syntax is not the constraint, so a local `JSON.parse` proves nothing; `scripts/__tests__/keycloak-realm-schema.test.mjs` fails the build on any `_`-prefixed key at any depth across every `*-realm.json` in the keycloak directory, and realm settings must be documented in the README instead.

Removing a client from a realm export requires removing every reference to it, not just the client object: a dropped client that still appears in `roles.client[<id>]` or `scopeMappings` makes `--import-realm` abort in production mode with `App doesn't exist in role definitions: <id>` and crash-loop `keycloak-service`. The ROPC client `mcm-bff-test` illustrates the asymmetry — it exists in the dev and CI realms but not in `prod-realm.json` — and it is no longer unused in the throwaway sense: the agent integration suite and the DAST job log in through it, so its secret is minted at bring-up, pinned into the realm import, and re-exported to the later steps, which therefore must not read it from `stacks/auth.env`.

The committed `prod-realm.json` keeps a `${BASE_DOMAIN}` placeholder (in the `movie-collection-manager` client's redirect URIs and web origins) that is rendered at deploy to a gitignored concrete file pointed to by `PROD_REALM_FILE`. The render must use `sed 's|${BASE_DOMAIN}|<domain>|g'`, not `envsubst`, because the realm JSON also contains 32 Keycloak `${role_*}` / `${client_*}` i18n placeholders that `envsubst` would expand and corrupt; the `sed` form touches only the literal `${BASE_DOMAIN}`.

Password policy is dropped from the CI realm export because Keycloak 26.6+ enforces a realm's `passwordPolicy` against imported user credentials (26.5 silently skipped it), so a realm that both carries a production-strength policy and seeds a user with a plaintext `${E2E_TEST_PASSWORD}` aborts a fresh `--import-realm`. `prod-realm.json` retains the policy because it seeds no user credential, so its import is unaffected; password strength is validated client-side in the E2E suite.

There is no hand-maintained authoritative source for the dev realm: `scripts/export-ci-realm.mjs` captures the live `grumpyrobot` topology through the Keycloak Admin API partial-export and sanitizes it into `ci-realm.json`, substituting every confidential client's secret with a `${ENV_VAR}` placeholder resolved from the container env at import and throwing if any secret-bearing client lacks a placeholder mapping — so a masked `**********` secret cannot be committed unnoticed. It also reconstructs `service-account-<clientId>` users with their role mappings, because a partial export omits service-account role mappings and a naive import would produce service accounts that mint tokens authorizing nothing. `dev-realm.json` is derived from that contract, and `scripts/check-realm-consistency.mjs` runs in the guardrails gate to fail on drift in realm name, app-client set, or `e2e-test-user` presence — deliberately without requiring byte equality, since redirect URIs and token lifespans may differ.

On the dev side, `node scripts/gen-dev-secrets.mjs` mints the realm/client secrets into the gitignored `stacks/auth.env`, and `node scripts/gen-dev-env.mjs` projects the same `KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET`, `KEYCLOAK_SERVICE_CLIENT_SECRET`, `AGENT_SUBJECT_TOKEN_CLIENT_SECRET`, `E2E_ROPC_CLIENT_SECRET` and `E2E_TEST_PASSWORD` values into the BFF env files so the imported realm's client secrets equal the dev BFF's secrets by construction (the invariant CI achieves by feeding the realm import and `.env.docker` from one set of forge secrets). Before writing anything, the projection verifies the service account's client-credentials grant and the ROPC password grant against the running realm and exits with code 2 without writing if the realm refuses a credential — writing the files would prove only that the values reached disk.

Any confidential Keycloak client whose secret is not pinned in the realm JSON receives a freshly generated random secret at import, so after a new volume import the generated secrets must be read from the Keycloak admin console and copied into the matching Komodo Variables. A value that is merely present but does not equal the deployed realm's client secret fails late and elsewhere: the BFF's RFC 8693 mint returns HTTP 401 `invalid_client`, the gateway then proceeds without a subject token, `needs_token` tools short-circuit with "No caller identity", and the observable symptom is an agent that falls back to TMDB and cannot resolve the user's collection.

The prod Keycloak admin console is published on host port 19099, not the dev/CI 8099: prod and the CI runner share one host under two rootless Docker daemons publishing into one host port space, and a `0.0.0.0:8099` prod bind overlapping CI's existing Keycloak on the loopback port 8099 crash-looped `prod-auth` for 6 h on 2026-07-06. Feature 029 moved the port into the prod-reserved 19000-19099 range and the admin console is served under a separate `KC_HOSTNAME_ADMIN` (the tailnet admin address, never the public host); the bind is `0.0.0.0` because the rootless daemon starts before `tailscaled` at boot, so a tailnet-IP bind silently fails, and tailnet-only exposure is preserved by the host firewall.

The prod container `keycloak-service` lost its `backend-network` attachment on reboot on 2026-07-06, coming back attached only to `edge-network` and `keycloak-network`, which broke mc-service's OIDC/JWKS discovery of `keycloak-service` (`dns error … Try again`). A manual `docker network connect` is only a one-off that the next reboot can lose; the durable remedy is a Komodo `prod-auth` redeploy, which recreates the container with the full network set already declared in `compose.prod.yaml`. Feature 029 additionally makes the intra-stack `keycloak-network` compose-managed rather than external, so Keycloak and its Postgres are created and attached atomically on every `up` even if the shared external networks hit the rootless re-attach race.

`KC_HOSTNAME` pins a stable token issuer regardless of the host a request arrives on, while `KC_HOSTNAME_BACKCHANNEL_DYNAMIC=true` lets backchannel endpoint URLs (token, JWKS) resolve from the incoming request — so the container BFF can perform the refresh-token grant over the internal network while the issuer stays fixed. Without the pin, the containerized BFF's refresh grant is rejected with `invalid_grant: Invalid token issuer`; the authorization_code login works regardless, because only the refresh grant validates a pre-issued issuer against the request host.

There is no cross-project `depends_on` between the local `auth` and `mcm` stacks (removed in feature 020), so `auth` must be brought up before the `mcm` `app` profile manually. The failure mode is not a crash or a hang: mc-service runs OIDC discovery and the JWKS fetch in a background task, binds and serves immediately, and rejects every protected request with 401 while `/health` still answers — so a backend that looks healthy but refuses every login means Keycloak is unreachable. This is pinned by `unauthenticated_401_is_returned_even_when_keycloak_is_unreachable` in the mc-service integration suite, which also exists to stop the test harness's readiness gate from being simplified away.

Client redirect URIs and web origins are realm state, not application config: `add-container-redirect-uris.mjs` idempotently adds the containerized-BFF callback and `login?verified=true` origins (dev container `:8082`, TLS `:8443`) to the `movie-collection-manager` client, and the mobile app-link/custom-scheme callback is the same kind of realm entry — its absence breaks on-device login only after the browser redirect, not at login time.

The CI runner is a PERSISTENT host, so `app-ci` force-removes the app containers and the stateful data volumes — `keycloak-store-postgres-data` among them — before provisioning each run: Keycloak's `--import-realm` uses IGNORE_EXISTING, so a realm left in place would never pick up a `ci-realm.json` change, and stale Mongo/Redis data breaks E2E idempotency. Image build caches are deliberately preserved so the rebuild stays fast. Without that reset step a committed realm edit would silently not reach CI.

`KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME` / `KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD` create the initial `admin` user only when the realm database has no admin, so the hardened posture is to log in once, create a named admin with 2FA and delete the bootstrap user — after which the values are inert. They must nevertheless stay configured: they are fail-fast `${VAR:?}` references, so removing the lines breaks every redeploy, and a fresh database deploy needs them to create the first admin at all.

The production admin console, served on the tailnet under its own `KC_HOSTNAME_ADMIN`, still sends its OIDC and session-check ("3rd party check") iframe to `KC_HOSTNAME` — the public auth origin. Until that public route resolves, opening the tailnet console fails with a third-party-check iframe timeout, so the failure is a missing public route rather than a broken admin login.

The realm's built-in default role is still named `default-roles-jumbleknot` in every committed realm variant even though the realm is `grumpyrobot` — the legacy organization name was intentionally retained — so a `default-roles-*` name that does not match the realm name is expected state, not drift.

`verify/verify-fresh-realm-seed.mjs` is the end-to-end acceptance check for the from-scratch dev seed: it force-removes the Keycloak containers, wipes and recreates `keycloak-store-postgres-data`, re-mints the dev secrets and brings `up-auth` up, then asserts with a real ROPC password grant as `e2e-test-user` against the `mcm-bff-test` client — a grant that can only succeed if the imported realm, the seeded user and the client secrets in `stacks/auth.env` all agree. Containers are removed before the volume so the wipe actually takes effect; the external volume is otherwise still referenced and the old Postgres password survives.

The refresh path keeps deliberate coverage that does not depend on the token lifespan: `agent-session-refresh.spec.ts` clears the `mcm_access_token` cookie explicitly rather than waiting for expiry, so it proves the 401 → refresh → retry recovery chain on a real browser-PKCE session regardless of the realm's `accessTokenLifespan`.

The `${BASE_DOMAIN}` render path is documented inconsistently with what is actually run: `compose.prod.yaml` and `.env.prod.example` describe rendering `prod-realm.json` with `envsubst` restricted to `BASE_DOMAIN`, while the runbook and README record the hand-run `sed 's|${BASE_DOMAIN}|<domain>|g'` as the command in use. Both touch only the literal `${BASE_DOMAIN}` and leave Keycloak's `${role_*}` / `${client_*}` i18n placeholders intact; a reader following only the compose comment has no warning about the unrestricted-`envsubst` corruption the restricted form exists to avoid.

The `keycloak-service` service head pins its image by tag AND digest (`quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.8.1@sha256:a78d6b79…`), identically in the dev/base `infrastructure-as-code/docker/keycloak/compose.yaml` and in `compose.prod.yaml`, and declares `depends_on: keycloak-store-postgres: condition: service_healthy` — so the container is not started until its own Postgres answers the `pg_isready -U keycloak -d keycloak` healthcheck, and a Keycloak that is up but cannot reach its database is a Postgres problem rather than a Keycloak one. The pin-by-tag-and-digest rule for production compose files is stated in the server-setup runbook.

The Keycloak container's command diverges by environment: `start-dev` in the base `compose.yaml` and in both the dev and CI overlays, but `start` (production mode) plus `--import-realm` declared in `compose.prod.yaml` itself. Relatedly, prod runs `restart: always` on both `keycloak-service` and `keycloak-store-postgres` where the base file uses `unless-stopped`, because the host's shutdown drain stops every container to `Exited (0)` and `unless-stopped` declines to restart a container that was stopped when the daemon returns — so on this host `always` is what actually makes a reboot hands-off, a property `scripts/check-prod-restart-policy.mjs` now enforces on every long-running prod service.

The keycloak README's one-minute `--import-realm` proof runs the importer against the same `26.8.1` image the compose files pin, so a green run is a version-parity check as well as a schema/deserialisation one — but it still verifies only the realm against that image, not the image's own behaviour: the Keycloak 26.6+ change that made a realm's password policy apply to imported user credentials was a server behaviour change no realm edit could have revealed.

Both prod auth-reachability invariants are self-enforcing CI gates rather than documentation alone: `scripts/check-prod-ci-port-collision.mjs` compares prod and CI/dev published host ports by NUMBER (a `0.0.0.0` prod bind collides with a CI bind on the same port regardless of the CI bind's host IP) and exits non-zero on any overlap, while `scripts/check-prod-restart-policy.mjs` forbids `unless-stopped` and a missing `restart:` on every long-running service in every `compose.prod.yaml` (only one-shot init/seed containers may use `no`/`on-failure`). The `guardrails` workflow runs each with `--selftest` first and then as a scan, so reintroducing the 2026-07-06 port overlap or the pre-feature-030 restart policy fails CI instead of the next deploy or reboot.

The production admin address is stack-supplied and the old bind-prefix variable is retired at every layer: the `prod-auth` block in `komodo/stacks.toml` sets `KC_HOSTNAME_ADMIN=http://[[TAILNET_HOST]]:19099` in its `environment` (which Komodo writes into the stack's gitignored `.env.prod`), `compose.prod.yaml` consumes it as `${KC_HOSTNAME_ADMIN:?…}` on the tailnet admin host, and `.env.prod.example` documents the same variable at the same prod-reserved port. `KC_ADMIN_BIND_IP` is gone from all three: feature 028 dropped it from the compose port bind and the stack stopped passing `KC_ADMIN_BIND_IP=[[TS_ADMIN_IP]]` on 2026-10-12 (item #727) — until then Komodo wrote it into `.env.prod`, which the keycloak compose loads with `env_file:`, so it reached the container as a `KC_*` variable naming no Keycloak option. The effective admin URL is therefore whatever `.env.prod` sets (`:19099` on this host), and no longer has to be read around a stale comment.

The two retired bind-prefix variables are the two halves of one operational rule: a Komodo stack `environment` key can outlive the compose that read it. `KC_ADMIN_BIND_IP` was prunable because both its consumer (feature 028's compose port bind) and its producer (the `prod-auth` block in `infrastructure-as-code/komodo/stacks.toml`, which stopped passing it on 2026-10-12, item #727) went away; `TS_ADMIN_IP` followed the same path one day later — no compose file had read it since feature 028 made the operator-UI binds `0.0.0.0`, the `prod-observability` block stopped passing it on 2026-10-13 (item #727), and the operator checklist records the Komodo Variable itself as removed. Neither name appears in `stacks.toml` any more, and the remaining tree-wide hits are guard selftest fixtures and historical comments rather than a stack or compose that reads them. The durable lesson is that removing a variable on the strength of "the bind is gone" is what breaks the next deploy — the stack `environment` line has to go first, and until it does the Variable must stay seeded even though nothing reads it.

`ensureClientRedirectUris(uris, keycloakClientId = env.keycloakClientId)` in `frontend/mcm-app/src/bff-server/keycloak.ts` is the runtime counterpart to the committed redirect URIs: `GET /bff-api/auth/init` calls it on app mount with the complete list (web OAuth callback, verified-email redirect, the native `mcm-app://` login callback, the backup-consent callback, the account-deletion step-up callback, and that flow's own native scheme URI), and it authenticates as the BFF service account, reads the live client, and PUTs it back with `[...existing, ...missing]`. The write being ADDITIVE is the property under guard; a module-level `Set` keyed by client id makes the call one-shot per client per process, marked only on a successful run, and the route makes a second call when `env.backupConsentClientId` names a client other than the login client so the consent callback is registered on that client too — a URI registered only on the login client is refused outright once the consent round trip is authorized as the consent client. `tests/integration/backup-consent-redirect-uri.integration.test.ts` asserts against a real Keycloak that the pre-existing URIs survive a call, not merely that the new one appeared, because a list-replacing write would silently unregister every unnamed flow and surface only when someone hit that flow, at Keycloak, with nothing pointing back at the change.

An infra-image CVE allowlist entry in `security/infra-images/allowlist.yaml` suppresses a finding only when its `image` regex matches the scanned `repo:tag` AND its `id` regex matches the advisory id AND the entry has not expired — so an entry keyed to a pinned version (or version plus digest) stops matching once the pinned image is bumped, re-blocking instead of inheriting the previous suppression. That is how the Keycloak allowlist entries were discharged rather than renewed: the bump itself was the remediation and the entries were deleted, because a re-keyed entry would have matched nothing and failed the gate's UNMATCHED ENTRIES check, and deletion is also the direction that restores blocking if the advisory returns.

The README's realm-import proof command does not name every placeholder the committed realm declares: it passes `MCM_BFF_TEST_CLIENT_SECRET` where the ROPC client expects `${E2E_ROPC_CLIENT_SECRET}`, and never sets `AGENT_GATEWAY_CLIENT_SECRET` or `MC_SERVICE_CLIENT_SECRET`. The import still succeeds and still prints `Realm 'grumpyrobot' imported`, because Keycloak leaves an unresolved `${...}` intact rather than failing the import — the same behaviour that preserves the realm's own `${role_*}` / `${client_*}` i18n keys. The proof therefore proves the realm deserializes; it does not prove every secret placeholder resolved, so the env-var names must be read against the realm rather than trusted.

The realm's client roles are read by two independent enforcement points that neither trusts the other: the BFF extracts them from the decoded JWT's `resource_access[clientId].roles`, and mc-service deserializes its `Role` enum out of the same claim for a `KeycloakAuthLayer<Role>` that checks only the JWT signature and audience, with a separate `require_app_role` middleware applying the `mc-user` OR `mc-admin` rule that the layer's own `required_roles` cannot express (it requires every role listed). A valid token carrying neither role is therefore authenticated and then refused with 403 rather than 401.

The app does not fetch the realm's OIDC discovery document. `use-keycloak-auth.ts` supplies expo-auth-session a static `DiscoveryDocument` — authorize, token, revoke, logout, userinfo — built from the configured issuer, because a client-side discovery fetch fails with a CORS "failed to fetch" in browser environments and Keycloak's endpoint structure is standardized; the issuer is itself derived as `${KEYCLOAK_URL}/realms/${realm}`. A wrong Keycloak URL therefore breaks the login redirect directly instead of surfacing as a discovery error, and it is the server-side OIDC discovery that must come from the internal origin.

The committed realm variants differ in brute-force protection as well as password policy: `prod-realm.json` sets `bruteForceProtected: true` while `dev-realm.json` and `ci-realm.json` both set it to `false`, because the throwaway realms seed known test users whose passwords the E2E suites re-use across runs — so a brute-force lockout there would break the suites rather than protect a user.

The scheduled-backup consent round trip — a separate OIDC flow carrying `scope=openid offline_access` whose result is stored as a standing permission and never turned into a session — runs as its own Keycloak client selected by `BACKUP_CONSENT_CLIENT_ID` (`mcm-backup-consent`, present in all three committed realm variants and set in CI's generated BFF env), and falls back to the login client with a one-time `backup_consent_shared_client` warning when unset. The separation is required by a measured Keycloak 26.8.0 session behaviour: the browser already holds the member's SSO cookie, so Keycloak answers the consent from the existing session and attaches the offline grant to it, and revoking a grant issued to the LOGIN client — by `/revoke`, by the admin API, with or without `prompt=login` — removes that client from the session, so the member's still-locally-valid access token then fails the agent subject-token exchange with `invalid_token`/`subject_token validation failure` (surfacing as "No caller identity") and the next refresh fails with `Session not active`. A grant issued to a separate client detaches only that client and the session survives, which makes this a production defect rather than a test artefact.

Two properties make the consent-client switch safe to roll out and both are enforced in code rather than by convention: grants are always used as the client that issued them — `credentialsFor(refreshToken)` reads the stored token's unverified `azp` claim and returns that client's id and secret, so grants made before the switch keep working with no stored-data migration, and an `azp` matching neither client gets the login identity that Keycloak then refuses, failing the grant as unusable rather than presenting a secret that does not belong to it — and the consent client reuses the login client's `${KEYCLOAK_CLIENT_SECRET}` in every realm variant, because the BFF is the sole custodian of both, while `BACKUP_CONSENT_CLIENT_SECRET` exists so production can pick a separate value later without a code change. The client itself is confidential and standard-flow-only (`directAccessGrantsEnabled`, `implicitFlowEnabled` and `serviceAccountsEnabled` false, PKCE `S256`), carries the same `mc-service-audience` mapper as the login client because an unattended run calls mc-service with a token minted from it, and `prod-realm.json` declares it without a secret so Keycloak generates one.

A user needs the `offline_access` role to grant backup consent: Keycloak supplies it through the realm's `default-roles-jumbleknot` composite, which Admin-API-created users inherit but users imported from realm JSON do not unless the import grants the default role — which is why the committed `e2e-test-user` and `e2e-admin-user` carry `realmRoles: ["default-roles-jumbleknot"]` alongside their `movie-collection-manager` client roles. Without it the consent round trip fails as a blank page after sign-in, with nothing naming the missing role. Relatedly, an established realm does not gain `mcm-backup-consent` from a realm JSON edit, because import is `IGNORE_EXISTING`: the client must be created in the running realm before `BACKUP_CONSENT_CLIENT_ID` names it, and the BFF never creates it itself.
